name: xz

patches.reason: Global (not target_overrides.windows-scoped, since the patch system only supports one global list) but OS-guarded at the C preprocessor level via CRT_TARGET_OS_WINDOWS, so it is a genuine no-op on Linux/macOS, where the __attribute__((constructor)) path already works correctly (verified). On Windows, lld-link does not reliably merge multiple static-archive-derived plain (non-$-grouped) .ctors/.dtors contributions into one contiguous, correctly-bracketed region -- confirmed empirically with a minimal, isolated reproduction outside liblzma entirely (a trivial constructor inside a .a archive, linked the same way, silently never runs). ./configure's own HAVE_FUNC_ATTRIBUTE_CONSTRUCTOR probe is a compile-only ac_fn_c_try_compile test (not even a link test), so it always reports 'yes' for this toolchain regardless of the archive-linking gap. Undefining it forces liblzma's own, already-designed-for-exactly-this-situation 'First Call Resolution' fallback (see crc32_fast.c and the four other files using the same CRC32_SET_FUNC_ATTR pattern), which needs no constructor/.ctors support at all -- the dispatch function pointer starts pointed at a lazy resolver called on first use.

notes: Scoped to liblzma only for this first pass: --disable-xz/--disable-xzdec/--disable-lzmadec/--disable-lzmainfo/--disable-lzma-links/--disable-scripts skip the xz command-line tool family (which pulls in getopt_long, sandboxing (seccomp/Capsicum/pledge/landlock), and console/locale handling well beyond what a library-only consumer like a future curl/pcre2 port would need). Revisit if a later port genuinely needs the xz CLI itself, not just liblzma.

--disable-nls avoids a gettext/libintl dependency this sysroot doesn't provide. --disable-doc skips Doxygen-generated API docs (no doxygen in this toolchain). --enable-sandbox=no is defensive (the xz CLI's own knob; harmless with --disable-xz). --enable-threads=posix is explicit rather than the default 'yes' auto-detection, since liblzma's multithreaded encoder/decoder should use this project's own real <pthread.h> on every OS, not a native Win32 threading path ('win95'/'vista') this PAL doesn't implement.
Uses GNU Libtool for the shared build, same as zlib.json/libpng.json -- the Windows-specific libtool/MinGW-detection fixes already live in tools/crt-port-build.py's make_env(), not per-recipe.

target_overrides.windows.cflags undefines _WIN32/_WIN32_WCE/__WIN32__/WIN32/__CYGWIN__ (same technique as every other Windows recipe in this directory) plus __MINGW32__ specifically for this recipe: unlike the other Windows recipes, xz's own src/common/sysdefs.h and src/common/mythread.h both branch on `#ifdef __MINGW32__` for real MinGW-w64-specific code this sysroot doesn't have an equivalent for -- `#include <_mingw.h>` (a real mingw-w64 header this project doesn't ship, since it isn't a full mingw-w64 distribution) and `#define sigset_t _sigset_t` (mingw-w64's own winpthreads doesn't have a real POSIX sigset_t, unlike this project's own <signal.h>, which already provides a real, working one -- the remapping macro just breaks it). Undefining __MINGW32__ keeps xz on its plain POSIX/pthreads path against this sysroot's real signal.h, which is what it actually needs.

FOUND AND FIXED ALONG THE WAY, NOT liblzma-specific: this port's own configure+make+install succeeded on the very first real attempt on Linux (x86_64, WSL Ubuntu 20.04 + clang-18), producing a working liblzma.a/liblzma.so.5.8.3. But the first real attempt to actually *use* the built library (a standalone lzma_easy_buffer_encode()/lzma_stream_buffer_decode() round-trip test, matching the verification pattern already established for zlib/libpng/bzip2) segfaulted at a null function pointer inside lzma_crc32(): liblzma's CRC dispatcher (src/liblzma/check/crc32_fast.c) picks its implementation once via `static void crc32_set_func(void) __attribute__((__constructor__))`, which the linker places into the ELF .init_array section -- and this project's crt1 startup never ran .init_array at all, on any of the three OSes, for the executable entry point. (A *shared* library's own .init_array is a completely different, unaffected mechanism -- the OS's own dynamic linker runs that automatically when the .so/.dylib/.dll loads -- which is exactly why this had never surfaced before: every prior port that got this far linked shared, not static.) Root-caused and fixed for Linux: libc/src/arch/linux/common/init_fini_array.c adds __crt_run_init_array()/__crt_run_fini_array(), called from crt1.S right before `call main` and from libc/src/exit.c right before process termination, linked directly into every Linux executable via a new crt1_init_array.o startup object. See HISTORY.md's dated entry for the full writeup. Windows and macOS still lack the equivalent fix -- see TODO.md.

A SECOND apparent bug (encoding a larger buffer hanging inside this project's own malloc() with the lock's raw value read back as garbage) turned out, after further investigation with gdb watchpoints, to NOT be a CRT/PAL/liblzma bug at all: it was a buffer overflow in this session's own throwaway verification program, not in anything shipped. The test built its input string with a snprintf() loop that accumulated the return value into a running length without ever checking it against the destination buffer's remaining size; once the accumulated length exceeded the buffer, `remaining = buffer_size - accumulated_length` (both size_t) underflowed to a huge unsigned value, so the next snprintf() call was handed an effectively unbounded size limit and wrote straight past the end of a `static` buffer -- trampling whatever the linker had placed after it in BSS, which happened to include malloc's own lock. Traced to certainty with a hardware watchpoint on the lock (`watch *(int*)&heap_lock`): each corrupting write's return address was `buffer_putc <- vsnprintf <- snprintf <- main`, i.e. this test program's own frame, not libc/liblzma, and the corrupted bytes decoded to literal fragments of the test's own format string ("xz/l...", from "CRT xz/liblzma port..."). Fixed the test (bounds-checked the accumulation, capped the loop) and re-ran: liblzma's real match-finder allocations (hundreds of KB up to ~512 MB at preset 9|EXTREME) all succeed cleanly, and a full compress/decompress round trip at preset 9|EXTREME with LZMA_CHECK_CRC64 produces byte-for-byte correct output, verified against both the static (liblzma.a) and shared (liblzma.so.5, with `ldd` confirming every dependency resolves to this project's own sysroot/port install dirs) build. No CRT/PAL fix was needed for this one -- it never existed outside the test harness. Linux is `shared-pass`.

windows: configure-pass, not shared-pass -- builds clean (static libbz2.a/liblzma.a-equivalent and shared liblzma-5.dll/lzma.lib, both via crt-port-build.py --use-crt-shell) after the __MINGW32__/RC/w32res fixes above, but actually calling the library crashes. Confirmed directly, not presumed: a standalone test showed a trivial lzma_version_string() call working fine, while the first real lzma_easy_buffer_encode() call segfaults -- on both the static and shared build -- in the exact same 'first real call into the CRC dispatcher' shape as the Linux .init_array bug this same port already found and fixed (see that note above and TODO.md). Strong circumstantial evidence it is the identical root cause reaching Windows, since every prior port that reached real verification here linked shared (where the OS loader runs a DLL's own constructors automatically) -- but not confirmed with a debugger the way the Linux case was, and not fixed this session. Checked what the fix would need to look like: PE constructors compile into a bare `.ctors` section for this toolchain (confirmed via `llvm-objdump -h` on a real __attribute__((constructor)) test), the GNU/MinGW convention, not MSVC's `.CRT$XCU` family -- and `.ctors` has no ELF-style automatic linker-provided start/end boundary symbols, so a correct fix needs the same `-1`-sentinel-object technique real mingw-w64 crt0 uses (a small 'begin' object linked immediately after crt1.o and a 'end' object linked last, each contributing a -1 value to the merged .ctors section, with the startup walker reading from the begin symbol's own address until it hits -1) -- deliberately not attempted this session: getting the link-order sandwich wrong would silently walk garbage memory as function pointers instead of failing loudly, and this already-long investigation was better stopped at 'confirmed and well-characterized' than pushed into a rushed, unverified platform-specific fix. Tracked as its own TODO.md item.

UPDATE, same session: the general .init_array/.fini_array gap referenced above is now fixed and verified on Windows -- see HISTORY.md's dated entry and TODO.md's dedicated item for the full writeup. It needed bracketing TWO separate, simultaneously-live constructor/destructor conventions, not the single .ctors/.dtors one assumed in the note above: this project's own CMake-native builds (as opposed to tools/crt-cc's --target=*-w64-mingw32 port builds, which do use .ctors/.dtors as expected) turned out to use the MSVC-ABI convention (.CRT$XCU/.CRT$XTX) instead, since they compile with plain clang and no explicit --target override. Verified via a new permanent regression test (tests/init_array_test.c) and a full local Windows ctest run (82/82).

UPDATE, later same session: re-ran xz's own Windows round trip and it STILL crashed even after the general .init_array fix above -- root-caused to a second, deeper, genuinely distinct lld-link limitation, not a leftover from the first bug. Isolated with a minimal, xz-independent reproduction (a trivial __attribute__((constructor)) function inside a standalone .a archive, linked the exact same way tools/crt-cc links liblzma.a): lld-link does NOT reliably merge multiple static-archive-derived plain (non-$-grouped) .ctors/.dtors contributions into one contiguous, correctly bracketed region the way GNU ld's default linker script guarantees via its explicit KEEP(*crtbegin.o(.ctors)) / KEEP(*(.ctors)) / KEEP(*crtend.o(.ctors)) ordering rules -- lld-link has no equivalent mechanism for COFF/PE. Confirmed directly: the sentinel begin/end markers land immediately adjacent to each other (an empty bracketed range) regardless of whether the real archived entry is placed before, after, or even bundled into the very same archive as the sentinels -- the archive-sourced entry consistently lands somewhere else in the image entirely (verified by locating its exact file offset via a raw pointer-value search through the linked binary). This affects the GNU-ABI (.ctors/.dtors) convention specifically, used by every tools/crt-cc port build; the MSVC-ABI ($-grouped .CRT$XC*/.CRT$XT*) convention this project's own CMake-native builds use is NOT affected (confirmed separately: lld-link's alphabetical $-suffix sorting is insertion-order-independent by design, unlike plain-section merging). Given this is a genuine lld-link limitation (not something fixable by rearranging this project's own sentinel objects) and liblzma's own CRC32/CRC64 dispatch code already ships a portable, purpose-built fallback for exactly this situation (crc32_fast.c/crc32_small.c/crc64_fast.c/crc64_small.c/lz_encoder.c's CRC32_SET_FUNC_ATTR pattern -- a 'First Call Resolution' lazy dispatcher used whenever HAVE_FUNC_ATTRIBUTE_CONSTRUCTOR is undefined, needing no constructor support at all), the fix routes around the lld-link gap instead of trying to work within it: a new build.patches entry undefines HAVE_FUNC_ATTRIBUTE_CONSTRUCTOR in src/common/sysdefs.h, guarded by #if defined(CRT_TARGET_OS_WINDOWS) so it is a genuine no-op on Linux/macOS (where the constructor path already works correctly and stays untouched). configure's own HAVE_FUNC_ATTRIBUTE_CONSTRUCTOR probe is a bare ac_fn_c_try_compile compile-only test (not even a link test), so it always reports 'yes' for this toolchain regardless of the archive-linking gap the probe has no way to see -- hence overriding it after the fact via a header patch rather than trying to make ./configure itself detect 'no'. Verified: full round trip (preset 9|EXTREME, LZMA_CHECK_CRC64, 256 KB real match-finder-exercising input, byte-for-byte compare after decode) now passes on Windows against BOTH the static (liblzma.a) and shared (liblzma-5.dll via lzma.dll.lib) build, rebuilt clean through the real crt-port-build.py pipeline (not just the isolated repro). Windows: shared-pass.

UPDATE, macOS verification: configure/make/install now succeeds on real macOS aarch64 through the CRT sysroot after tools/crt-cc learned to treat `-r`/`-Wl,-r` as a relocatable-link mode instead of an executable/shared-library link. GNU Libtool's Darwin path uses repeated `ld -r` partial links; adding executable-only startup objects, `-dead_strip`, entry flags, and CRT libraries there was wrong, and ld64 rejects `-r` with `-dead_strip`. A second Darwin-specific partial-link issue also surfaced: with xz's `-fvisibility=hidden`, ld64 lowered `private external` definitions to local symbols during the partial link, leaving same-output external references unresolved at final dylib link. Passing `-Wl,-keep_private_externs` only for macOS relocatable links preserves the needed internal references without changing final executable/shared links. Verified past build success: a standalone CRT-linked program ran `lzma_easy_buffer_encode()` at preset 9|EXTREME with LZMA_CHECK_CRC64, then `lzma_stream_buffer_decode()`, and byte-for-byte compared the 256 KiB output against the original input against BOTH installed `liblzma.a` and `liblzma.5.dylib` (otool confirmed the shared test loads this port's installed dylib). macOS: shared-pass.

dependencies added "make" (2026-08-25, found and fixed via porting/recipes/freetype.json's own matching note -- see that file for the full trail): this recipe's own build.system is "configure", and tools/crt-port-build.py always builds the `make` port first for any configure-system recipe, but tools/fetch_ports.py only fetches what a recipe's own `dependencies` array declares -- an empty array here meant a fully standalone `port-fetch-xz`/`port-build-xz` (no other recipe fetched first into the same port-tests/src/ tree) would fail with `source not found: .../toolchain-make-...`. Fixed the same way as libffi.json/zlib.json already do.
